parts.s: Names India as a Union of States and sets out its territory. Parliament can admit or set up new States, form new States and change the areas, boundaries or names of existing ones, with matching changes to the First and Fourth Schedules.

Sets out who became a citizen of India when the Constitution began, including people who migrated to or from Pakistan and people of Indian origin living abroad. A person who voluntarily takes foreign citizenship is not a citizen, and Parliament regulates citizenship by law.

f: Saving of Certain Laws
Ins. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 3 (w.e.f. 3-1-1977).
parts.s: Lists the Fundamental Rights: equality, freedom (including speech, and protection of life and personal liberty), the right to education, rights against exploitation, freedom of religion, and cultural and educational rights. It also saves certain laws and gives the right to constitutional remedies to enforce these rights.

Lists the Directive Principles the State must apply in making laws, though no court can enforce them, such as a welfare-based social order, equal justice and free legal aid, village panchayats, fair work conditions and a living wage, a uniform civil code, early childhood education, protecting the environment, and separating the judiciary from the executive.

f: Part IVA
Ins. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 11 (w.e.f. 3-1-1977).
parts.s: Sets out the Fundamental Duties, all in a single article (Article 51A).

s.t: Powers, Privileges and Immunities of Parliament and its Members

parts.s: Sets up the Union government: the President and Vice-President, the Council of Ministers and the Attorney-General; Parliament and how it passes laws and handles money; the President's power to issue Ordinances; the Supreme Court; and the Comptroller and Auditor-General.

s.t: Powers, privileges and immunities of State Legislatures and their Members

ch.t: The High Courts in the States

f: The States
The words "IN PART A OF THE FIRST SCHEDULE" omitted by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, s. 29 and Sch. (w.e.f. 1-11-1956).
parts.s: Sets up government in the States: the Governor, the Council of Ministers and the Advocate-General; the State Legislature and how it passes laws and handles money; the Governor's power to issue Ordinances; the High Courts; and subordinate courts, including district judges.

parts.t: The States in Part B of the First Schedule
f: Part VII
Omitted by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, s. 29 and Sch. (w.e.f. 1-11-1956)
parts.s: This Part has been omitted. Its title covered the States in Part B of the First Schedule.

f: The Union Territories
Subs. by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, s. 17, for the heading "THE STATES IN PART C OF THE FIRST SCHEDULE" (w.e.f. 1-11-1956).
parts.s: Covers how Union territories are run, including local Legislatures or Councils of Ministers for some of them, special provisions for Delhi, the administrator's power to issue Ordinances, the President's power to make regulations, and High Courts for Union territories.

f: Part IX

Original Part IX relating to "The territories in Part D of the First Schedule and other territories not specified in that Schedule" was omitted by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, s. 29 and Sch. (w.e.f. 1-11-1956) and subsequently ins. by the Constitution (Seventy-third Amendment) Act, 1992, s. 2 (w.e.f. 24-4-1993).
parts.s: Covers Panchayats: the Gram Sabha, how Panchayats are formed and made up, reservation of seats, their term, disqualifications, powers, taxes and funds, a Finance Commission to review their finances, audit and elections. Courts are barred from interfering in their electoral matters. The Part also applies to Union territories, but not to certain tribal and hill areas and States, and it had a transitional rule for older Panchayat laws.

f: Part IXA
Part IXA ins. by the Constitution (Seventy-fourth Amendment) Act, 1992, s. 2 (w.e.f. 1-6-1993).
parts.s: Covers Municipalities: how they and Wards Committees are formed, reservation of seats, their term, disqualifications, powers, taxes and funds, a Finance Commission, audit and elections. It also provides committees for district planning and metropolitan planning.

f: Part IXB
Part IXB ins. by the Constitution (Ninety-seventh Amendment) Act, 2011, s. 4 (w.e.f. 15-2-2012).
parts.s: Covers co-operative societies: how they are incorporated, the number and term of board members, board elections, supersession of boards, audit, general body meetings, members' right to information, returns, and offences and penalties, with rules for multi-State co-operative societies and Union territories. In 2021 the Supreme Court held that this Part applies only to multi-State co-operative societies, because the amendment that added it was not ratified by half the States.

Covers the administration of Scheduled Areas and Tribal Areas, and allows an autonomous State to be formed from certain tribal areas in Assam, with its own local Legislature or Council of Ministers or both.

parts.t: Relations between the Union and the States
parts.s: Divides law-making power between Parliament and the State Legislatures, including residuary powers, goods and services tax, and when Parliament can make laws on State List matters. It also covers administrative relations, inter-State river water disputes and an inter-State Council.

s.t: Distribution of Revenues between the Union and the States

ch.t: Property, Contracts, Rights, Liabilities, Obligations and Suits

f: Chapter Iv.—right to Property
Ins. by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 34 (w.e.f. 20-6-1979).
parts.s: Covers public finance: taxes only by law, the Consolidated and Contingency Funds, sharing of taxes between the Union and States, the Goods and Services Tax Council and the Finance Commission. It also covers borrowing, property, contracts and suits, and the right not to lose property except by law.

parts.t: Trade, Commerce and Intercourse within the Territory of India
parts.s: Declares freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse throughout India and sets its limits, including restrictions Parliament and the States can impose and the saving of laws for State monopolies.

parts.t: Services under the Union and the States
parts.s: Covers people serving the Union and the States: recruitment, conditions of service, tenure, rules on dismissal, removal or reduction in rank, and the All-India services. It also sets up Public Service Commissions for the Union and the States and sets out their members and functions.

f: Part XIVA
Ins. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 46 (w.e.f. 3-1-1977).
parts.s: Allows administrative tribunals, and tribunals for other matters, to be set up.

Places control of elections in an Election Commission and lets Parliament and State Legislatures make election laws. No one can be left off the electoral roll only because of religion, race, caste or sex, and elections to the House of the People and State Assemblies use adult suffrage. Courts cannot question delimitation laws, and an election can be challenged only by an election petition.

parts.t: Special Provisions Relating to Certain Classes
parts.s: Reserves seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, and once delimitation is done for women, in the House of the People and State Assemblies, and sets when reservation ends; Anglo-Indian nomination has lapsed. It sets up National Commissions for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Backward Classes, covers claims to government posts, and lets the President notify who counts as Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and backward classes.

ch.t: Language of the Supreme Court, High Courts, etc.

parts.s: Covers the official language of the Union and the States, the language between States and with the Union, and the language of the Supreme Court, High Courts and Acts. It also covers mother-tongue teaching at primary stage, a Special Officer for linguistic minorities and developing Hindi.

Covers Proclamations of Emergency and their effects, the Union's duty to protect States against external aggression and internal disturbance, failure of constitutional machinery in a State, suspension of Article 19 and of the right to go to court for Fundamental Rights (except Articles 20 and 21) during emergencies, and financial emergency.

Gathers miscellaneous provisions: protection of the President and Governors, protection for publishing legislative proceedings, disqualification from paid political posts, Rulers of Indian States and the end of their privy purses, major ports and aerodromes, the effect of a State not following Union directions, and definitions and interpretation.
Gives Parliament the power to amend the Constitution and sets out the procedure for doing so.

f: Temporary, Transitional and
Subs. by the Constitution (Thirteenth Amendment) Act, 1962, s. 2, for "TEMPORARY AND TRANSITIONAL PROVISIONS" (w.e.f. 1-12-1963).
parts.s: Contains temporary, transitional and special provisions, including Article 370 on Jammu and Kashmir (which since 2019 only applies the whole Constitution there) and special provisions for Maharashtra, Gujarat, Nagaland, Assam, Manipur, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Sikkim, Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh, Goa and Karnataka. It also covers continuing existing laws and the changeover when the Constitution began.

parts.t: Short Title, Commencement, Authoritative Text in Hindi and Repeals
f: Short Title, Commencement, Authoritative
Ins. by the Constitution (Fifty-eighth Amendment) Act, 1987, s. 2 (w.e.f. 9-12-1987).
parts.s: Gives the Constitution's short title and commencement, provides for an authoritative text in Hindi, and deals with repeals.

p: WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a {1}[SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC] and to secure to all its citizens:
LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship;
EQUALITY of status and of opportunity;
and to promote among them all
FRATERNITY assuring the dignity of the individual and the {2}[unity and integrity of the Nation];
IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION.
f: Subs. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s.2, for "SOVEREIGN DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC" (w.e.f. 3-1-1977).
Subs. by s. 2, ibid., for "Unity of the Nation" (w.e.f. 3-1-1977).

sch.t: The States and the Union territories
sch.s: Lists the States and Union territories and the territory each covers, mostly by reference to the Acts that formed or changed them. It serves Articles 1 and 4.

sch.t: Provisions as to the President, Governors, Speakers, Judges and the Comptroller and Auditor-General
sch.s: Sets out the salaries, allowances and privileges of the President and Governors, the presiding officers of Parliament and State Legislatures, Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, and the Comptroller and Auditor-General. Most of the rupee amounts shown have since been raised by laws made by Parliament (the President, for example, now gets five lakh rupees a month). It serves Articles 59, 65, 75, 97, 125, 148, 158, 164, 186 and 221.

Gives the forms of oath or affirmation for Union and State Ministers (office and secrecy), candidates for and members of Parliament and State Legislatures, Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, and the Comptroller and Auditor-General. It serves Articles 75, 84, 99, 124, 148, 164, 173, 188 and 219.

sch.t: Allocation of seats in the Council of States
sch.s: Allots the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) seats filled by representatives of each State and Union territory, 233 in total, ranging from 31 for Uttar Pradesh to 1 for several smaller States and Puducherry. Members nominated by the President come on top of these. It serves Articles 4(1) and 80(2).

sch.t: Provisions as to the Administration and Control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes
sch.s: Sets out how Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes are run in States other than Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. The Governor reports to the President and can direct that any Act shall not apply to a Scheduled Area, or shall apply with changes. The Governor can also make regulations, for example restricting tribal land transfers or controlling money-lending, but only after consulting the Tribes Advisory Council (up to twenty members, about three-fourths of them Scheduled Tribe members of the State Assembly) and with the President's assent. The President declares Scheduled Areas, and Parliament can amend the Schedule by ordinary law. It serves Article 244(1).

sch.t: Provisions as to the Administration of Tribal Areas in the States of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram
sch.s: Provides for autonomous districts and regions in the tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. Each district has a District Council of up to thirty members (no more than four nominated by the Governor, the rest elected; Bodoland in Assam can have up to forty-six), and each region has a Regional Council. The Councils can make laws on local matters such as land, forests, marriage and social customs, which take effect only with the Governor's assent, and can also run village courts and levy certain taxes. It serves Articles 244(2) and 275(1).

Contains the three subject lists used under Article 246 to divide law-making power. Parliament makes laws on the Union List (such as defence, foreign affairs, citizenship, railways, banking and insurance), State Legislatures on the State List (such as police, public order, public health, agriculture and land), and both on the Concurrent List (such as criminal law, marriage, education, forests and electricity). Any subject not listed anywhere belongs to Parliament.

Lists 22 languages: Assamese, Bengali, Bodo, Dogri, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Kashmiri, Konkani, Maithili, Malayalam, Manipuri, Marathi, Nepali, Odia, Punjabi, Sanskrit, Santhali, Sindhi, Tamil, Telugu and Urdu. It serves Articles 344(1) and 351.

sch.t: Validation of certain Acts and Regulations
sch.s: Lists Acts and Regulations, mostly on land reform, tenancy and land ceilings, that Article 31B protects from being struck down for conflicting with Fundamental Rights. A few entries have since been removed. The Supreme Court has held that laws added on or after 24 April 1973 can still be tested against the basic structure.

sch.t: Provisions as to disqualification on ground of defection
sch.s: Sets out when a member of Parliament or a State Legislature is disqualified for defection, such as voluntarily giving up party membership, voting or abstaining against the party's direction without permission (unless the party forgives it within 15 days), or an independent joining a party after election. There are exceptions for mergers agreed to by at least two-thirds of the party's legislators and for presiding officers. The Chairman or Speaker decides, and it serves Articles 102(2) and 191(2).

sch.t: Powers, authority and responsibilities of Panchayats
sch.s: Lists 29 subjects, including agriculture, minor irrigation, drinking water, rural housing, roads, education, health and sanitation, and the public distribution system, on which a State Legislature may by law give Panchayats powers and responsibilities. It serves Article 243G.

sch.t: Powers, authority and responsibilities of Municipalities, etc.
sch.s: Lists 18 subjects, including urban planning, land use and building rules, water supply, sanitation and solid waste management, fire services, slum improvement and registration of births and deaths, on which a State Legislature may by law give Municipalities powers and responsibilities. It serves Article 243W.

themes.q: What rights does the Constitution guarantee me?
themes.d: The rights in Part III that every person or citizen holds against the State, and how to enforce them in court.

themes.q: What does the Constitution expect from me?
themes.d: The Fundamental Duties added in Part IVA, from respecting the flag to protecting the environment.

themes.q: Who counts as a citizen of India?
themes.d: Citizenship at the start of the Constitution and Parliament's power to regulate it.

themes.q: What is the government meant to work towards?
themes.d: The Directive Principles: aims such as fair wages, free legal aid, education and village panchayats. Courts cannot enforce them, but the State must apply them in making laws.

themes.q: How does Parliament pass a law?
themes.d: Bills, the two Houses, money bills, joint sittings, the President's assent and ordinances.

themes.q: Who runs the government?
themes.d: How the President is elected, the Council of Ministers led by the Prime Minister, and the powers each holds.

themes.q: How do the Supreme Court and High Courts work?
themes.d: Who the judges are, how long they serve, how they can be removed, and what cases each court hears.

themes.q: Who can vote and who runs elections?
themes.d: The Election Commission, adult suffrage, electoral rolls, qualifications for MPs and MLAs, and disqualification for defection.

themes.q: Who makes laws on what?
themes.d: How law-making power is divided between Parliament and the States through the Union, State and Concurrent Lists.

themes.q: How is public money raised and spent?
themes.d: Taxes only by law, the Consolidated Fund, the annual budget, GST, the Finance Commission and the Comptroller and Auditor-General.

themes.q: What happens in an emergency?
themes.d: National emergency, President's rule in a State, financial emergency, and what happens to rights meanwhile.

themes.q: How does local government work?
themes.d: Village panchayats and urban municipalities: elections, reserved seats, five-year terms, finance commissions and their functions.

themes.q: How does the Constitution protect disadvantaged groups?
themes.d: Reservations, abolition of untouchability, commissions for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and backward classes, and seats for women.

themes.q: How can the Constitution be amended?
themes.d: The procedure and majorities needed to amend the Constitution, and the record of amendments in this edition.

themes.q: What can't Parliament change?
themes.d: Provisions the Supreme Court has ruled part of the basic structure, which no amendment can destroy, and those most likely to be part of it. The basic structure page explains how this is worked out.

themes.q: What are India's official languages?
themes.d: Hindi in Devanagari script as the official language of the Union, the use of English, regional languages and the 22 languages of the Eighth Schedule.

themes.q: Which States have special arrangements?
themes.d: Special rules for particular States and regions, from Maharashtra and Gujarat to Nagaland, Sikkim and Karnataka, and Article 370.

themes.q: What protections do government employees have?
themes.d: Recruitment and conditions of service, protection against dismissal without inquiry, and Public Service Commissions.

themes.q: How are Union territories and Delhi governed?
themes.d: Administration of Union territories, special provisions for Delhi, and the list of territories in the First Schedule.

themes.q: What does the Constitution say about women?
themes.d: Equality and non-discrimination on grounds of sex, special measures for women, maternity relief, and seats reserved for women in Parliament, State Assemblies and local bodies.

themes.q: What protections do children have?
themes.d: The right to free and compulsory education, bans on child labour and trafficking, care in early childhood, and the duty of parents to provide education.

themes.q: How does the Constitution treat religion?
themes.d: Freedom of conscience and worship, the rights of religious denominations and minority institutions, and the State's duty to treat all faiths alike.

themes.q: What does the Constitution say about the environment?
themes.d: The State's duty to protect forests and wildlife, every citizen's duty to protect nature, and how powers over land, water and forests are shared between governments.

themes.q: How are tribal communities and areas protected?
themes.d: Special administration for Scheduled and Tribal Areas, reserved seats, the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes, and provisions for States in the North-East.

themes.q: Who keeps the government in check?
themes.d: Constitutional bodies that audit, advise and oversee: the Comptroller and Auditor-General, the Election Commission, the Finance Commission, Public Service Commissions and national commissions.

themes.q: What are my rights if I am arrested or tried?
themes.d: Protection against retrospective punishment and self-incrimination, the right to life and liberty, safeguards on arrest and preventive detention, legal aid, appeals and pardons.

themes.q: How free is speech in India?
themes.d: The freedom of speech and expression and its limits, the freedom of legislators to speak in the House, reporting of proceedings, and what happens to the freedom in an emergency.

themes.q: Who is responsible for education?
themes.d: The fundamental right to education, rights of minorities to run institutions, religious instruction in schools, mother-tongue teaching, and how education is shared between the Union and the States.

themes.q: What does the Constitution promise workers?
themes.d: The freedom to form unions and pursue any occupation, bans on forced and child labour, and the State's goals of fair wages, humane conditions and worker participation.

themes.q: Is property a fundamental right?
themes.d: Property was a fundamental right until the Forty-fourth Amendment (1978) took effect in 1979; it is now protected by Article 300A. Land reform laws are shielded by Articles 31A to 31C and the Ninth Schedule.

next.headline: No amendment Bill is close to a final vote. The next amendment is most likely to be about how Lok Sabha seats are shared among the States and when seats reserved for women start. The surest date is 25 January 2030: reserved seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes end then unless Parliament extends them, and it has extended them every time before.

when.why: At the pace of the last ten years, six Acts in ten years, there would be about a 45% chance of at least one Act in any year. The chance is lower now. No Bill is near a final vote, the Government's last attempt failed in April 2026, and the main open question waits for Census 2027, whose counting runs into March 2027.

when.by: By June 2029, when this Lok Sabha's term ends
when.why: Seats reserved for women can start only after constituencies are redrawn on the new census, and the freeze on seat shares ends with the same census. Both make seats a likely subject before the next general election. The April 2026 vote showed there is no agreement yet on how.
Article 334 ends reserved seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes on that date. Parliament has extended the deadline before each of the seven times it fell due.
